meta.title: A Comparative Study of Reconstruction-Based Deep Learning Models for Spacecraft Telemetry Anomaly Detection

abstract: Anomaly detection in spacecraft telemetry is critical for ensuring mission safety and operational reliability. Telemetry streams are typically high-dimensional multivariate time-series characterized by complex temporal and cross-channel dependencies, making robust modeling challenging. This paper presents a comparative study of deep learning architectures for reconstruction-based anomaly detection in spacecraft telemetry. We evaluate representative models, including USAD (Unsupervised Anomaly Detection), OmniAnomaly, TranAD (Transformer-based Anomaly Detection), and Anomaly-Transformer, under unified experimental settings using public spacecraft telemetry benchmarks as well as a real operational satellite dataset. Experimental results show that Transformer-based architectures generally achieve strong detection performance across the evaluated datasets. In particular, Anomaly- Transformer consistently provides the best balance between precision and recall, achieving the highest F1-scores on both benchmark and real mission telemetry data. These findings suggest the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in modeling long-range temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions, providing practical insights for selecting suitable deep learning models for spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection.

blocks.html: Reliable anomaly detection in spacecraft telemetry is essential for ensuring mission safety, fault diagnosis, and operational continuity. Modern spacecraft continuously generate high-dimensional multivariate telemetry streams that reflect the dynamic state of onboard subsystems. Detecting abnormal behavior from these time-series signals is challenging due to complex temporal dependencies, non-stationary characteristics, and the scarcity of labeled anomaly data [1]. Traditional rule-based or statistical approaches often struggle to generalize across varying operational modes and subtle fault patterns.

Deep learning has emerged as a powerful alternative for time-series anomaly detection [2]. In particular, Transformer architectures [3] have demonstrated strong capability in modeling long-range temporal dependencies through self-attention mechanisms [4]. At the same time, various non-Transformer architectures, including recurrent and autoencoder-based models, have been widely adopted for multivariate time-series anomaly detection. Despite their success, a systematic comparison between Transformer-based and non-Transformer architectures in spacecraft telemetry monitoring remains limited.

Deep learning-based anomaly detection methods are generally categorized into prediction-based and reconstruction-based paradigms. In spacecraft telemetry monitoring, reconstruction-based approaches are particularly attractive due to the scarcity of labeled anomaly data. These methods learn representations of normal operational behavior and detect anomalies through elevated reconstruction errors.

Reconstruction-based anomaly detection has evolved from early encoder-decoder models such as LSTM- (DAGMM) [6], to multi-scale architectures such as Multi-Scale Convolutional Recurrent Encoder-Decoder (MSCRED) [7]. More recent developments incorporate stochastic latent modeling [8] and dual-decoder strategies [9], reflecting continuous progress in modeling complex multivariate time-series data.

blocks.html: In this paper, we conduct a systematic comparative analysis of Transformer-based and non-Transformer architectures within the reconstruction-based anomaly detection paradigm for spacecraft telemetry. We evaluate representative reconstruction models on publicly available spacecraft telemetry benchmarks as well as a real operational satellite dataset. Through consistent experimental settings, this study analyzes how different architectural mechanisms influence anomaly detection performance under realistic operational conditions.

In this study, we focus on reconstruction-based anomaly detection models, which are widely adopted in unsupervised time-series analysis due to their ability to learn normal operational patterns without requiring labeled anomalies. In this paradigm, anomalies are identified based on deviations between input telemetry signals and their reconstructed outputs.
We evaluate four representative deep learning models with distinct architectural characteristics.

USAD [9] is a dual autoencoder framework that alternately optimizes two reconstruction networks to enhance robustness. Its training scheme reduces overfitting by introducing adversarial-style reconstruction consistency, thereby improving anomaly discrimination in unsupervised settings.

OmniAnomaly [8] integrates gated recurrent units (GRU) with stochastic latent variables in a variational framework to capture complex temporal dynamics and uncertainty in multivariate time-series data. It models normal system behavior through probabilistic latent representations optimized via variational inference.

TranAD [10] is a Transformer-based architecture incorporating self-conditioning and multi-stage reconstruction. Through attention mechanisms and iterative refinement, TranAD enhances anomaly sensitivity by leveraging reconstruction residual feedback.

Anomaly-Transformer [11] introduces an association discrepancy mechanism that measures the divergence between prior and series associations within a self-attention framework. This enables explicit differentiation between normal and abnormal temporal dependencies while effectively modeling long-range cross-channel interactions.

For all models, anomaly scores are derived from reconstruction errors between the input and reconstructed signals, following each model’s original scoring formulation. Scores are aggregated at the timestamp level, and thresholds based on validation statistics are applied to determine anomalous events.

These four models were selected because they represent diverse reconstruction-based anomaly detection paradigms, including autoencoder-based, probabilistic recurrent, and Transformer-based architectures.

To evaluate anomaly detection performance under diverse spacecraft telemetry conditions, experiments were conducted on two publicly available benchmark datasets, SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) and MSL (Mars Science Laboratory) [12], along with an in-house spacecraft telemetry dataset referred to as Mission-K.

In SMAP and MSL, anomaly labels are provided as part of the benchmark dataset and correspond to telemetry intervals identified by NASA mission experts. For Mission-K, anomaly labels were generated based on satellite operation logs and engineering assessments.

SMAP and MSL. SMAP and MSL are widely used spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection benchmarks derived from NASA missions.For this study, the SMAP dataset includes 25 input channels with an anomaly ratio of 13.3%, while the MSL dataset includes 55 input channels with an anomaly ratio of 10.4%. Both datasets contain labeled anomalous events and are commonly used to evaluate multivariate time-series anomaly detection models.

blocks.html: Mission-K. To assess model performance under realistic operational conditions, we introduce an in-house spacecraft telemetry dataset, referred to as Mission-K for anonymity. Mission-K consists of GPS-related telemetry collected from an actively operating satellite and includes 29 input channels.

The dataset spans one month of mission data sampled at a 1-second interval. The training set comprises 20 days of normal operational data, while the test set consists of 10 days of telemetry containing both normal and anomalous segments. The anomaly ratio in the test set is approximately 3.8%, reflecting an imbalanced yet operationally realistic scenario.

An example telemetry signal from Mission-K with a highlighted anomaly interval is shown in Figure 1. The figure illustrates the temporal behavior of a representative telemetry channel during the anomalous period. The observed anomalies correspond primarily to contextual anomalies.

Prior to model training, telemetry data were preprocessed to ensure numerical consistency across channels. Categorical states (e.g., ENABLE/ON/VALID and DIS- ABLE/OFF/INVALID) were mapped to binary values (1 and 0), and missing values were filled using linear interpolation. The dataset was then divided into training and test sets, where min–max normalization was fitted on the training data and the same transformation parameters were applied to the test data.
Mission-K complements public benchmarks by representing genuine mission conditions and real anomaly occurrences in spacecraft telemetry.

To quantitatively evaluate anomaly detection performance, we report Precision, Recall, and F1-score. These metrics are computed by comparing predicted anomaly labels with ground-truth annotations at the timestamp level.

where TP and FP denote true positives and false positives, respectively. Precision reflects the proportion of correctly identified anomalies among all detected anomalies, indicating the reliability of anomaly alarms.
Recall is defined as
where FN denotes false negatives. Recall measures the ability of a model to capture actual anomalous events, which is critical in mission-critical spacecraft systems.

F1-score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall: F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall Precision + Recall. In highly imbalanced anomaly detection scenarios, F1score provides a balanced evaluation by jointly accounting for false positives and false negatives.
These metrics together characterize the trade-off between missed detections and false alarms, both of which are crucial considerations in operational spacecraft telemetry monitoring.

All models were implemented using PyTorch 1.8.1 with CUDA 11.1 and trained on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. To ensure a fair comparison, a unified experimental framework was applied across all architectures.
Multivariate telemetry data were segmented into fixedlength sliding windows of 100 time steps with a stride of

1. Each telemetry channel was independently normalized using statistics computed from the training set. In accordance with the unsupervised anomaly detection setting, only normal operational data were used during training.

For window-based reconstruction models (USAD, TranAD, and Anomaly-Transformer), each input window of length 100 was processed according to the model architecture. USAD reconstructs the entire input window, whereas TranAD and Anomaly-Transformer reconstruct the target timestep within the window. OmniAnomaly operates in a sequential timestep-wise manner using recurrent modeling without explicit window reconstruction, effectively processing data with stride-1 temporal updates.

Anomaly scores were primarily computed using the mean squared error (MSE) between the original input and the reconstructed output. Model-specific training objectives were configured as follows. USAD alternates the optimization of two autoencoders using reconstruction and adversarial-style consistency losses. OmniAnomaly incorporates variational inference with an MSE reconstruction loss and a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence term for latent regularization. TranAD employs MSE-based reconstruction with multi-stage refinement, while Anomaly-Transformer combines reconstruction loss with a KL-divergence-based association discrepancy term to enhance anomaly discrimination.

All models were trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10−4 and a batch size of 256 for up to 20 epochs. Early stopping with a patience of 10 epochs was applied based on validation loss to mitigate overfitting. A portion of the training data was reserved for validation and threshold estimation.

Cross-validation was not employed because anomaly detection was evaluated under a chronological time-series setting, where preserving the temporal order is essential to avoid information leakage between training and testing. Instead, a validation subset extracted from the training data was used for early stopping and threshold estimation. This strategy also helped reduce overfitting while ensuring that the test set remained completely unseen during model development.

During inference, anomaly scores were computed for each window and mapped back to timestamps. Detection thresholds were determined using validation statistics, and samples exceeding the threshold were classified as anomalous.

Table 1 summarizes the anomaly detection performance across the three datasets. On the SMAP and MSL benchmarks, Transformer-based models (TranAD and Anomaly- Transformer) generally achieve higher Precision and F1scores than non-Transformer architectures. In particular, Anomaly-Transformer obtains the best F1-score on both datasets, reaching 0.96 on SMAP and 0.93 on MSL. These results indicate the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in capturing complex temporal dependencies within multivariate telemetry streams.

On the Mission-K dataset, which represents real operational satellite telemetry with an anomaly ratio of 3.8%, all models achieve very high Recall values close to 0.99, indicating that most anomalous events are successfully detected across architectures. Compared to previous experiments with lower anomaly ratios, the performance gap between Transformer and non-Transformer models becomes smaller under this setting. Nevertheless, Anomaly-Transformer still achieves the highest overall F1-score (0.99), demonstrating the most balanced performance between Precision and Recall.

A similar trend can be observed in the AUC scores, where most models achieve values close to 1.0, suggesting that the anomaly score distributions are generally well separated. However, F1-score differences remain important for practical anomaly detection since they reflect the trade-off between false positives and missed detections under a fixed decision threshold.

Overall, while the increased anomaly ratio reduces the performance gap among models, the results consistently show that Anomaly-Transformer provides the most stable and reliable detection performance across both benchmark datasets and real spacecraft telemetry data.

The comparative results indicate that Transformer-based architectures generally achieve strong anomaly detection performance across the evaluated datasets. In particular, Anomaly-Transformer consistently attains the highest F1scores on SMAP (0.96) and MSL (0.93), demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling complex temporal dependencies in multivariate telemetry data. These observations suggest that attention-based architectures are beneficial for the evaluated telemetry datasets, particularly when long-range temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions are prominent.

On the Mission-K dataset, which represents real operational satellite telemetry with an anomaly ratio of 3.8%, all models achieve very high Recall values close to 0.99. Under this setting, the performance gap between Transformer and non-Transformer architectures becomes noticeably smaller compared to the benchmark datasets. Compared with SMAP and MSL, Mission-K contains anomalies that are more clearly distinguishable from normal operating conditions. In addition, GPS telemetry channels tend to exhibit relatively stable operational patterns with fewer mode transitions, making deviations easier to reconstruct. Consequently, even relatively simple reconstruction models achieve high detection performance, reducing the performance gap among architectures.

Nevertheless, Anomaly-Transformer still achieves the highest overall F1-score (0.99) on Mission-K, indicating that it maintains a slightly better balance between Precision and Recall compared to the other models. This suggests that attention-based mechanisms remain beneficial for robust anomaly detection even when anomalies are relatively distinguishable.

A comparison between the two Transformer-based models, Anomaly-Transformer and TranAD, provides additional insights. Although both architectures employ selfattention mechanisms, Anomaly-Transformer consistently achieves higher F1-scores across datasets. This performance difference may be attributed to the association discrepancy mechanism used in Anomaly-Transformer, which explicitly models the divergence between normal and abnormal temporal dependencies. By contrast, TranAD focuses primarily on iterative reconstruction refinement, which may be less effective in capturing subtle relational deviations across telemetry channels. These results suggest that explicitly modeling anomalous attention patterns can further enhance anomaly detection performance in multivariate time-series data.

From a practical perspective, the results indicate that Transformer-based models are promising candidates for spacecraft telemetry monitoring systems, particularly when complex temporal dependencies and subsystem interactions must be considered. Their ability to model global relationships across channels can provide more reliable detection in operational environments where anomalies may propagate across multiple subsystems.

However, several limitations should be acknowledged. Transformer models generally require higher computational and memory resources than conventional architectures, which may limit their direct applicability in onboard processing environments. In addition, the real operational dataset used in this study focuses primarily on GPS-related telemetry signals. While this provides a meaningful evaluation scenario, spacecraft systems include a wide range of subsystems and payload instruments with diverse operational characteristics.

Another limitation of this study is that architecture-specific hyperparameter optimization was intentionally omitted to maintain a fair comparison across all models. While this unified experimental protocol enables a consistent comparison of architectural characteristics, individual models may achieve improved performance under optimized hyperparameter settings.

Future work will extend the evaluation to telemetry data containing a broader variety of anomaly types and subsystem behaviors. In addition, architecture-specific hyperparameter optimization, repeated experiments, and statistical significance analysis will be conducted to better assess the robustness of the evaluated models and verify whether the observed performance differences are statistically meaningful.
